title: How relationship‐quality with family, peers, and teachers relates to adolescents' bicultural identity integration ( BII )
abstract: Abstract Family, peers, and teachers are important socialization agents that often represent different cultural orientations for ethnically minoritized adolescents. This study examined how positive relationships to these socializing agents contribute to Bicultural Identity Integration (BII) among 226 minoritized adolescents in Germany ( M age = 12.9, 51.1% female, diverse national backgrounds, 27.1% first‐ and 72.9% second‐generation immigrants). Multinomial logistic regression analyses tested whether positive family climate, peer acceptance, and positive teacher‐generated classroom climate—independently and in combination—predict membership in five previously identified BII trajectories [two time points, 2 years apart, 2019–2021, identified through latent class growth analysis] ( p < .001, R 2 = .238). Findings revealed that, particularly, the combination of multiple high‐quality relationships had synergistic effects in predicting membership in the more resolved BII trajectory subgroups High Integrated BI ( n = 49, 21.6%) and Conflict Resolution ( n = 18, 7.9%), while lower relationship quality predicted membership in the less resolved, Ambivalent BII ( n = 69, 30.5%) subgroup. Hence, sustained positive engagement with multiple socialization agents provides minoritized adolescents with relational scaffoldings necessary to navigate and harmonize multiple cultural identities.
